question: Is there a remedy for foolishness?
summary: Proverbs 22:15 and Proverbs 27:22 sit in the same book and give opposite verdicts on whether foolishness can be driven out of a person. 22:15 says foolishness is bound in the heart of a child but the rod of correction will drive it far from him — corporal discipline as the cure. 27:22 says you can grind a fool in a mortar with a pestle along with wheat and his foolishness still will not depart from him — the fool is incorrigible. Same wisdom collection, two incompatible anthropologies of folly.

reconcile.connective: Matthew Henry ties the two proverbs together directly, reading the rod of correction in 22:15 as effective only while a child's character is still forming, and the incorrigible fool of 27:22 as one whose folly has already hardened past that window.

discrepancy.connective: Form-critical scholar R. N. Whybray argues Proverbs is an anthology of originally separate collections that were never redactionally harmonized, so a pair like this preserves genuinely rival ancient wisdom voices on whether character can be reformed rather than one settled doctrine.

pd_work.resource: John Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874)
pd_work.author: John W. Haley
pd_work.note: Haley treats this exact pair under the heading "Folly,--treatment" (two columns: "Folly remediable." / "Folly remediless."), p. 278, quoting Prov 22:15 and 27:22 side by side and resolving the tension with the identical age-based distinction MHC uses: "'Foolishness,' in the first text, is the incipient waywardness which belongs...to children, and may be corrected by suitable discipline. The 'fool' in the second text, is the grown-up fool, whose folly is past cure."

excerpts.attribution: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-14)
excerpts.excerpt_text: Solomon had said (Pro 22:15), The foolishness which is bound in the heart of a child may be driven out by the rod of correction, for then the mind is to be moulded, the vicious habits not having taken root; but here he shows that, if it be not done then, it will be next to impossible to do it afterwards; if the disease be inveterate, there is a danger of its being incurable.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: MHC explicitly names Pro 22:15 by citation and states the age/inveteracy-based harmonization for why 27:22 says the fool's folly will not depart -- directly on this row's tension.
excerpts.source_note_text: Solomon had said (Pro 22:15), The foolishness which is bound in the heart of a child may be driven out by the rod of correction, for then the mind is to be moulded, the vicious habits not having taken root; but here he shows that, if it be not done then, it will be next to impossible to do it afterwards; if the disease be inveterate, there is a danger of its being incurable. Can the Ethiopian change his skin? Observe, 1. Some are so bad that rough and severe methods must be used with them, after gentle means have been tried in vain; they must be brayed in a mortar. God will take this way with them by his judgments; the magistrates must take this way with them by the rigour of the law. Force must be used with those that will not be ruled by reason, and love, and their own interest. 2. Some are so incorrigibly bad that even those rough and severe methods do not answer the end, their foolishness will not depart from them, so fully are their hearts set in them to do evil; they are often under the rod and yet not humbled, in the furnace and yet not refined, but, like Ahaz, trespass yet more (Ch2 28:22); and what remains then but that they should be rejected as reprobate silver?
